utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next witness is Major Mark Bower of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire. He served in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the British Battalion in Vitez from April of 1993 until November of 1993. You heard earlier this week from his then commanding officer, Brigadier Alastair Duncan, who was then the commanding officer of the British Battalion. He was at the time a captain, this is Major Bower, and he was responsible as a liaison officer for assisting humanitarian organisations, such as the Red Cross, with their work in the Lasva Valley. In his testimony, he will tell you very briefly of a visit that he made in late April to the village of Ahmici, and he will tell you what he saw and the conclusions that he reached. He will next tell you of how, on a reconnaissance mission, in the town of Busovaca, in the municipality of Busovaca, he came across a group of extremely well-armed professional troops of the HVO who he discovered to be a group called "the Jokers." Next he will tell you of his knowledge of HVO military formations in the Lasva Valley and his understanding of the command structure of the HVO. He will tell you of how, in his opinion, how effectively he thought the command structure functioned. He will give you his impression of the Hotel Vitez as a military headquarters. He will then speak to you of his assistance of both the sick and injured within the town of Vitez, both Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims. He will tell you of a number of visits that he made to two Bosnian Croat hospitals, one in Vitez and one in Novi Bila. He will tell you of the Stari Vitez enclave, a Muslim pocket isolated in Vitez by the time he arrived after the fighting in April. He will tell you of his attempts to bring in humanitarian assistance to that enclave, and he will tell you of a campaign of attrition waged by the HVO against that Muslim pocket and how civilians, predominantly women and children, were the victims of a sniper and indiscriminate mortar fire campaign from the HVO, and he will tell you how this happened 400 metres from Colonel Blaskic's headquarters in Vitez. He will tell you very briefly of his visits to the town of Kruscica, another Muslim pocket partially isolated with some access to Bosnian government controlled territory, and how attempts to gain access with humanitarian assistance to this area was thwarted by the manipulation of the local Bosnian Croat civilian population by the HVO. He will tell you of his knowledge of what he came to know of in the Lasva Valley of HOS units, and he will tell you of the command chain that he perceived in respect of those witnesses, in respect of those troops. He will mention very briefly to you the death of Dobrilla Kolaba who -- I think you heard about that in some length from Brigadier Duncan. This was an interpreter who worked for him. He will tell you of his witness to trench-digging by individuals who appeared to be under the control of HVO soldiers. In the final part of his testimony, he will tell you of what he saw of an attack on the village of Grbavica. He will describe to you a professional, well-coordinated attack against the Bosnian forces in that area and the civilian populations that were located there, the Bosnian Muslim civilian population. He will tell you of the civilians that were rescued by the British Battalion for fear of them being killed in the attack, and he will tell you of his witness to HVO soldiers and civilians looting the Bosnian Muslim area of Grbavica immediately after the attack. Lastly, he will tell you, very briefly, at the end of his tour, how he witnessed the aftermath of the HVO attack on the village of Stupni Do in the municipality of Vares. The testimony is, I think, relevant to paragraphs 3 and 4 of the indictment, paragraph 5.2 of the indictment; Count 1, the persecution; Counts 2 to 4, unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects; Counts 5 to 10, wilful killing and causing of serious injury; Counts 11 to 13, destruction and plunder of property; Counts 15 and 16, inhumane and cruel treatment of detainees. I estimate that my examination-in-chief will be in the region of an hour, possibly shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. If I've understood correctly, I think that Major Bower, that is his testimony, in light of his speciality, has to be focused mainly on humanitarian assistance. That seems to be the essential point to me and, at the same time, the command structure, and then the attacks that he might have seen and the consequences of this. But especially somebody who can address the issue of humanitarian assistance for which he was in some way responsible, and he was able to see, in your opinion at least, a certain number of blockages. Those are the essential points, as well as the command structure. As Judge Riad has just reminded me: humanitarian assistance, command structure, consequences of certain attacks. Very well. We can have Major Bower brought in. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Major, do you hear me? Will you please recall your rank, your name, and your first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major Mark Bower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing, as long as it takes to read your solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. You may be seated. You have come at the request of the Prosecutor to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in a trial of the accused General Blaskic who is here in this courtroom. We know the general outline of what your testimony is, the essential points, and it is on those points that the Prosecutor will focus, and then there will be a cross-examination. But I know that you're familiar with these procedures because you come from a country which uses it. Without any further ado, let me give the floor back to Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Bower. Just a few preliminary questions. When I ask you questions, if you could address your answers to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you joined the army in 1983?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you joined the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire in 1985 after the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you've served in the United Kingdom, Kuwait, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Canada, Kenya, France, and the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you've done operational tours of duty in Northern Ireland, Iraq, Kuwait, and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you were, in fact -- you've seen combat duty in the Gulf War; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you served with the Prince of Wales' Regiment in Bosnia-Herzegovina from April of 1993 until November of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think the Prince of Wales' Regiment was the second British Battalion to serve in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think I'm correct in saying that you were based at the Stari Bila camp in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your responsibility when you were based in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I think you were a captain at the time.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. My duties were liaising between the British Battalion based in Stari Bila and mainly the aid agency, the ICRC, and some of the non-government organisations such as Pharmaciens sans Frontieres and Medecins sans Frontieres. I had also responsibility between travelling around the area, around the Lasva Valley, and assessing humanitarian aid requirements, and then I would pass it to UNHCR and other agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you're now a Major and a company commander?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you also were awarded by Her Majesty the Queen, The Queen's Gallantry Medal, after your service in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think we'll come on to why you received that gallantry award later in your testimony. Now, very briefly, if you could recollect for the court a visit that you made to the village of Ahmici at the end of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was as soon as I arrived in Bosnia -- the incident in Ahmici had happened, but it was the aftermath, the clearing-up option was still continuing, and I accompanied the Cheshire Regiment, who were still there at the time, into Ahmici to assist in recovery of some of the bodies which were still in the houses at the northern end of the town. The clearing-up operation was taking some time. There were fears that there may be unexploded ammunition in the area, so it was a military operation to clear it before attempting to retrieve the bodies. And so I went in to assist in collecting the bodies and then informing the family members in Zenica that we had found the remains of their family.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What opinion, what conclusion, did you reach at the time as to what had taken place in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It appeared to be a concentrated military effort onto a small town, village. It was -- or it appeared to be quite brutal in its execution in the fact that the majority of the houses were completely destroyed. No one would have been able to move into these houses as the majority of the roofs had fallen in and there were scorch marks from intense heat and fire on the outside of the buildings where the flames had come out through the windows. Although there were a few houses which were untouched and people were still living in those houses and later it was found out that these people were Croats and had lived in Ahmici and remained to live in Ahmici after the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence of defensive structures in that village?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I obviously can't comment on what was inside the buildings because of the destruction that had taken place, but I didn't see large trench systems or any large support weapon pits, large sort of earthworks, which would denote a large military installation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can move on to the next part of your testimony, and if the witness could be given the first exhibit, which is really a map to assist the court and to show the various locations that you were operating, and it has no particular significance. Mr. Registrar, what Exhibit number is this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 394.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think at the end of May of 1993, you made a visit to the municipality of Busovaca, and I think while you were there, you came across a group of soldiers. Can you describe that visit to the court and that group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was in early May, and I had spent the majority of the first two weeks in and around Travnik and Vitez, so decided to look around the area of Busovaca to assess the aid requirements in some of the more remote areas, and so decided to travel to the area which is marked 1 here (indicates), and I basically travelled to Busovaca and headed west up some mountain roads. I was in two Land Rover military vehicles which are soft skin. They are not armoured vehicles, and after maybe 15 minutes, having travelled down dirt tracks in wooded areas in the mountainous region, I came across a tree trunk which is across the road, blocking the road. And to the right of my vehicles, there were -- or there was a chalet, lodge, it was maybe 15 -- maybe 50 metres away from the track. The sound of the vehicles brought out a number of people from the hut and from behind it, 15 in total maybe. They approached the vehicles, and some of them, eight, nine of them, actually stayed 25 metres short of the vehicles and adopted fire positions with their weapons and pointed their weapons at us, and six or eight of them approached the vehicles. But we couldn't engage them in conversation; they ignored us. Two of them stood in front of me but wouldn't speak to me; the remainder went around and had a good look at both vehicles, the drivers, the commanders of the vehicles, and the people in the backs of them. They were quite menacing, they were well-equipped, well-armed with non-Yugoslav-manufactured weapons, non-Soviet bloc weapons, the majority of them had large hunting knives, and some had pistols as well. They were young, mid-20s, I would say. They had an air of professional military competence, but they were also quite menacing. My interpreter was Dobrilla Kolaba, and she attempted to engage them in conversation, but they were talking to themselves, again ignoring us, but very interested in us. After trying to explain to them why we were there, that all we wanted to do was pass through, Dobrilla Kolaba was quite anxious and said we should leave. When I tried to get further information as to why she just said, "We should leave and we should leave now" and she appeared quite anxious and agitated, so we got back into our vehicles and reversed down the track, because we couldn't turn the vehicles around, and went back to Busovaca where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have a subsequent discussion with her when you stopped about the nature of these troops that you just encountered?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I wanted to discuss what had happened because I had not seen her like that before, and she explained that this group were known as the Jokeri and that they were discussing whether they should kill us or whether they should let us go. She also stated to me that this group had been involved in Ahmici and that the insignia they had on them, which was a white skull and crossbones insignia on a headband, some were on badges, on patches on their combat jackets, signified belonging to this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were any of them wearing HVO badges?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I think one or two of them were wearing just the red and white chequered badge which I took to denote HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever receive further information about the involvement of this group in combat operations on the HVO Bosnian government front-lines?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Every night we had a discussion amongst all the liaison officers with our commanding officer, Colonel Duncan, and on occasions, the Jokeri were mentioned as being involved or seen in action around Novi Travnik and Travnik and Grbavica, and there was one report that they had been around Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the battalion come to some sort of a conclusion about what was the special nature of these troops, why they were used in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was assessed that this group were professional, dedicated, and clearly capable in military operations, and could bolster the generally conscript nature of the forces wherever the main effort at the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move on -- and I think it naturally moves on -- to your knowledge of military formations within Central Bosnia. Now, I know you were briefed on both Bosnian government forces and the HVO, but I'd like you to explain to the court what your knowledge was at the time of the HVO military structure within Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: We were briefed on arrival in Bosnia about both BiH and HVO chains of command. This enabled us to make the best use of our time when dealing with front-lines, military checkpoints, because we could understand their chains of command and who we should go and see in that area, the military commanders in that area, to seek assistance or permission to cross front-lines and whatever. I understood that in the Lasva Valley, the HVO headquarters was in Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any particular knowledge about the subordinate military formations in the Lasva Valley that were part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Only in the fact that I knew that geographical areas were responsible or were the responsibility of specific military groupings, but ultimately there was a link and a chain from the soldier to checkpoint through his local commander, ultimately reaching Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of who, during your tour of duty, was the commanding officer of the HVO located at Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any understanding of the extent of his command in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: As I understood it, he was responsible for HVO forces in the Lasva Valley where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you give sort of geographical marker points, your knowledge of the area, the geographical area, that that covered?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: From where I worked, certainly stretching from Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kruscica, the Lasva Valley pocket where we were based.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was really the limit of your knowledge because you didn't really travel much outside that area?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, did you ever have occasion to visit the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: On occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many times did you visit Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the operational tour, there was no requirement to visit it on a regular basis, but as the fighting increased, it became more and more necessary to visit. I would say in the six and a half months I was in Bosnia, maybe 40 or 50 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you give the court a description of your impression of Hotel Vitez as a military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was the impression of a professional working military headquarters, well-structured. When I went in, if I didn't have an arranged meeting with anybody, there would be somebody who I'd report to, I would wait, they would go and get somebody. It appeared to be a normal, what I would class, working, efficient military headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you had occasion to frequently travel, I think, through both HVO and Bosnian government-controlled checkpoints; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, based on your knowledge of your impressions within the Hotel Vitez and your transiting through checkpoints, can you explain to the Judges how effectively the chain of command functioned within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The checkpoints, the HVO checkpoints, certainly at the junction to the road to Vitez, when access was denied, a barrier was across the road and we were told we weren't allowed to enter. Negotiation would start with the checkpoint commander to be allowed to travel into Vitez to go to Hotel Vitez. Initially, the answer would be "No. No one is allowed in." But obviously I had asked to see the local checkpoint commander, his superior officer, and it appeared to me that they were talking by telephone or some other means of communication up the chain of command because, more often than not, we were allowed to travel through, which signified to me that there was a working chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever have experience with the civilian authorities and utilising them to gain access to particular areas?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Once when I was attempting to get into Kruscica, which is marked 4 on the map here, which is again a small Muslim enclave south of Vitez, I was stopped from travelling through to take a UNHCR aid convoy and to casualty evacuate some wounded people with the ICRC, and we were stopped by women and children blocking the road, standing in front of our vehicles. The average length of negotiations would be three to four hours and would invariably result in not being able to travel through. One particular occasion, the mayor of Vitez, I believe his name is Santic, and a liaison officer, Darko Gelic, came down to the checkpoint with a British Battalion liaison officer, Captain Whitworth, but they were unable to get the convoys through to Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So Mr. Santic had no authority to facilitate your access?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: He didn't appear to be, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you say that the military authorities had a firm grip in your area where you were assisting humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Whenever we wanted something actioned, we invariably went to the military chain of command rather than the civilian chain of command. It seemed to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When we're talking about the military, we're talking about the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there's one example that you have, and it's mentioned in your statement, of the coordination within the HVO chain of command, and a particular example of the International Committee for the Red Cross attempting to move aid from Mostar into Central Bosnia. Could you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: My duties included going to the ICRC every morning, and I listened to their briefs and they listened to mine, and on one morning they informed me that they had been told by the HVO in Novi Travnik that, if they did not receive aid, then the HVO in Mostar would stop any ICRC convoys coming up the route from Metkovic to Mostar to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did this indicate to you about the chain of command within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It showed a degree of communication but also cooperation and coordination over a distance to coordinate an effort or threat such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is quite usual within any sort of reasonably, well-developed military formation; is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can now move on with your testimony to the two Bosnian Croat medical facilities, the hospital in Vitez and the hospital in Novi Bila, and I wonder if you could explain to the court your involvement with those two institutions?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: During the summer, the fighting was, at times, intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is the summer of '93?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The summer of '93, and the main aid agencies, the UNHCR and the ICRC, would not travel where there was fighting for fear of taking casualties. So the British Battalion decided to get involved in casualty evacuation to save life, and that was my responsibility. In the Lasva Valley, there were two primary medical facilities that I was involved with. The one in Vitez seemed to be more of a clinic for the everyday medical needs of a community, from pregnancy, broken limbs, the everyday medical requirements, although it would treat battle trauma cases from the Vitez area, specifically just localised Vitez area. The primary battle trauma hospital was in Novi Bila in a church which was used as the hospital, and that could accommodate maybe 120 seriously wounded people, the majority of which were from battle trauma from the result of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were involved in a particular evacuation, a coordinated evacuation that was taking injured and sick people down to Split. I wonder if you can tell the court about that? I think this was the instance when you, in fact, were awarded the Queen's Gallantry Medal.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: There had been an offer to evacuate some 55 wounded people from Novi Bila to Kiseljak where they would then be put on helicopters and flown to Croatia for onward medical care. It took a degree of coordination because we had to travel through the BiH front-lines to get to Kiseljak. It took three or four days. The BiH wanted a list of names of who would be evacuated and they had to be identified. And the BiH provided a doctor to ensure that the right people with those medical complaints went on the transport. They were people who were very, very ill, who would probably have died if they had not have moved. The BiH could see what was going on and started to fire at the hospital with mortar rounds, although it was not particularly close. One of the hospital administrators told me that I had to leave some of the people off the transport, the nominated 55, and take some middle-aged and young men and some women and children who didn't appear to be injured. There was a rumour that these people had tried to buy places on this relief convoy, this evacuation, but I refused to let them on, and the administrator personally threatened that I would suffer if I didn't take these people. The discussion was cut short because the hospital was mortared and it took three direct hits from the BiH in the local area. They landed right next to the hospital where we were. So I continued to evacuate the seriously wounded from the hospital and get them onto the transport and we left as soon as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the other hospitals, the other Bosnian Croat hospitals in Vitez, the HVO-controlled hospitals, did you come across a number of victims of gunshot wounds, civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware by whom those people were injured?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: By BiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know from where?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly in the Novi Bila area, they were from around the front-lines in the western part of the Lasva Valley pocket. In the Vitez clinic, there were, again, a number of women, children who had suffered battle trauma, casualties, and they had been caused by the BiH in Stari Vitez, the Muslim enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, we naturally, I think, move on to Stari Vitez and if you can indicate on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, before we move to Stari Vitez, perhaps we would take a break. We have had a long morning. Twenty minutes now. Since this is about halfway through the testimony that Major Bowers is giving, perhaps we can divide the sequence into two and start again at 10.35. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please? Are all the technical problems okay? There are no technical problems, yes, everything is fine. Sorry for the slight delay. Thank you. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Bower, we left off in your testimony and we were just moving on to the Muslim enclave of Stari Vitez. Could you point out to the Judges on the map that's next to you that you've marked in your own hand your best recollection of the Muslim enclave of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It's marked as "Area 3" here on the map and it was to the south of the Travnik-Busovaca road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what your perception of the Stari Vitez enclave was at the time, why it existed?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was centred around the Muslim population of Stari Vitez near the mosque and it was made up of non-combatants and combatants. There were Bosnian army in there as well. They were unable to have freedom of access and exit of Stari Vitez to the remainder of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By whom was the access to Stari Vitez controlled?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were heavily involved, I think, in movement of casualties and provision of humanitarian aid to this region. I would like you to briefly give a summary of your six-month involvement with the people of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the aid agencies would not go anywhere where there was a danger to themselves, so it was left to me to assess humanitarian aid requirements and to conduct medical evacuations as a result of war fighting. Therefore, I would negotiate passage into Stari Vitez and, more importantly, negotiate the evacuation of casualties from Stari Vitez to the hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: With whom did you have to negotiate the movement of casualties and humanitarian aid in and out of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I had to go to Hotel Vitez to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any other way of getting into Stari Vitez, except by driving past Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: As can be seen on the map, there is one road running here which goes all the way through Stari Vitez, but before I arrived in Bosnia, at approximately this location on the road, the road was blocked by earthworks, some trailers from lorries, and also there were some explosive devices placed, some mines, placed on the earthworks. So no access by any vehicle could be made from the west. It had to be made from the east and, therefore, it had to go to what we termed the Vitez T-junction and follow the road round into Stari Vitez and pass Hotel Vitez to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the Witness can be shown Exhibit 395, I think that probably demonstrates the route that you're talking about into Stari Vitez. It's not completely on the ELMO but do you see the image in front of you on the TV screen?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you sufficiently demonstrate what you've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, the general area of Stari Vitez is in this area here to the left of the picture, and the access route along the yellow line which is here was the only way that any vehicles could be taken into Stari Vitez, so any casualty evacuation out of Stari Vitez or any humanitarian aid to go in had to travel down that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And past Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know where Hotel Vitez is?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It's just off --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Off the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: -- the screen to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you point to it?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: There. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Above the letter "E," there is a square; what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: In this general area here was the end of the HVO front-line and the Bosnian army front-line was around here. And in this area, in the latter part of the summer of '93, mines were placed across this road here and, I believe, down here which stopped again the freedom of movement of our vehicles into Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you're indicating also to the left of the letter "E," there was another mine when, in fact, it wasn't marked on here --

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- although you marked with your own hand on the main road above. Now, if you could explain to the court how you were involved in the evacuation of casualties from Stari Vitez over a six-month period and why those people were injured, what sex they were and what age they were, as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The casualties which I evacuated were from a house. It was a makeshift hospital which is in this area here of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's the sort of yellow mark at the extreme left?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: This house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it actually says "hospital," but it can't quite be seen.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: There. (Indicated). It was run by Dr. Enisa Mulalic whose husband was a doctor in Zenica. She had two nurses who assisted her and they cared for the general medical welfare of the community, but also they dealt with all the war trauma casualties which the fighting created. I evacuated the region of 50 to 60 people over my six and a half months in Stari Vitez. The majority were suffering from war trauma, gunshot wounds, shrapnel and blast injuries, and they could not receive the required medical aid in Stari Vitez. They would have died if they had stayed. Predominantly, they were women and children which I evacuated. There were some older men aged 50, 55. There were a few men of fighting age which were evacuated, again, because they would have died if they had stayed, but Dr. Mulalic understood the strict rules which I applied, and I used as a basis the ICRC rules that I would not move any military equipment so that anyone of combatant age who was very seriously ill must leave all his equipment behind. I would not move anyone with equipment or I would not move any friend to accompany him, so it was purely the wounded person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And all of these individuals were Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: From Stari Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's deal firstly with the gunshot injuries. What type of fire had caused those injuries?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Predominantly the gunshot wounds were caused by the 7.62 short round fired from AK-47 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it your view that these rounds had been fired by snipers?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The rounds were fired by people who were waiting for targets of opportunity and then they shot at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. What is the 7.62 short round? Can you help me what it is? We're not military experts.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Sorry, it is the round fired, the bullet fired, by the rifle, the AK-47 rifle, and the "7.62" is the diameter of the bullet, 7.62 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is it strictly military weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It's available for any use that has that calibre rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, a sniper doesn't necessarily need to be armed with a sniper rifle, does he? He can be armed with any weapon.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The idea that a sniper must have a telescopic sight and be well concealed, camouflaged, is not always the case. The term "sniper," as I would interpret it, is anyone who waits for a target of opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the blast injuries; what were they caused by?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The blast injuries were caused by indirect fire weapons such as mortars and, in the summer, there was a home-made mortar bomb which we, in BRITBAT, called the fire extinguisher bomb. It was the canister of a fire extinguisher that was ballistically thrown 100, 200 metres over the front-lines. It could be filled with petrol, something to ignite a fire, so it was incendiary, or a low level explosive to create a blast.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How indiscriminate were these weapons, in effect?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The people at the firing point of these weapons would not be able to see where the round would land because it was going over the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you're talking about a round, you're now talking about a fire extinguisher --

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: A fire extinguisher bomb or a mortar round. It is termed indirect. It doesn't travel in a straight line. It will go over the area, the ground it wishes to travel. The home-made device such as this fire extinguisher bomb was very unstable. It had no guiding fins, like a plane, to stabilise it in its flight. It was crude and inaccurate. And because it takes time to travel from the firing point to the detonation point, maybe as long as 10 to 15 seconds, no guarantee could be made of who would be in the target area when the bomb detonated. And because the firers could not see physically who was in that area when they fired it, it was indiscriminate and it caused a number of civilian non-combatant casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 82/7, please? It's a man holding a red canister.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 82/5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 82/5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Bower, do you recognise this device?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is what the British Battalion termed the fire extinguisher bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these were the devices that were being fired into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they were fired. On one occasion, this -- I don't know if it was this particular canister, but one was brought to the hospital where I was in Stari Vitez. There always seemed to be a need of the medical staff to show me where the people had been wounded or killed, to show me the bodies, to show me the injuries in case I didn't believe what was going on. It was to try and emphasise their situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've described this campaign over a six-month period of firing these devices on a sniper campaign. Was this being conducted by the HVO against Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Muslim people in Stari Vitez, how frightened were they?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It would fluctuate, depending on the level of fighting in Stari Vitez or around Stari Vitez, but generally, it was a feeling of despair among the civilians which I tended to deal with. The Merhamet representative in Stari Vitez, I believe her last name was Mrs. Halilovic, was always requesting assistance in humanitarian aid, generally baby food, bottles, sterilisation, sanitisation aid, and they generally felt that they just were holding on. They had enough assistance to survive, but that was all, they were surviving.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that the movement in and out of Stari Vitez was controlled by the HVO and that included aid, did it not, humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The aid into Stari Vitez was controlled by the Vitez T-junction checkpoint I mentioned earlier. A convoy of 10 or 15 tons of humanitarian aid would be in four or five large UNHCR or ICRC trucks. So it was conspicuous. It could not travel in unnoticed. The drivers of these vehicles were civilians and, therefore, they would not be taken into an area that was dangerous because of fighting. The UNHCR had had a representative shot dead in Stari Vitez as he sat inside his UNHCR vehicle. And so this made the aid agencies very cautious, and they wanted reassurance that they would be unhindered in taking aid into Stari Vitez. So, in effect, the enclave of Stari Vitez was controlled by the amount of aid, medical, food and also the evacuation of casualties out, it was very closely controlled by the checkpoints to the degree that I was aware that if I did not have the permission to evacuate people from Stari Vitez, I would be putting those people at risk when we got to the Vitez checkpoint and we attempted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I know you evacuated a large number of people, but if you could just give the Judges one or two examples of the age and sex of the victims you evacuated from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The first victim I evacuated was an 11-year-old girl who had been shot in the head by a 7.62 millimetre round one afternoon in May. I believe it was the 21st of May. She was very seriously ill. The round had passed through her head. It wasn't until darkness that night that the message was received by the British Battalion that there was this seriously ill casualty, and I evacuated her that night. Other casualties in July, I think it was the 18th or 19th of July, there were, again, three casualties caused by a blast bomb; one male, he was about 40 to 45; a woman, middle-aged, and a child, I don't know what age. The man died in the hospital in Stari Vitez while I was there. He had severe shrapnel injuries to his abdomen and chest. The woman had shrapnel injuries to her face and throat and was having difficulty breathing and was very ill. The child had shrapnel injuries to her face and was suffering from shock but it was severe shock, almost in a traumatic state of shock. I evacuated the woman and the child and left the dead man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this was the normal course of events over all these evacuations over six months?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It fluctuated between gunshot wounds, blast injuries, and occasionally there would be the normal medical problems created, pregnant women with difficulties or old people who relied on insulin who were diabetics who required medical aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of the number of women and children that were killed in Stari Vitez by sniper fire and blast injury?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I couldn't put a finger on it. If somebody was killed, I would be told about it, but I could do nothing so I wouldn't remove the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But are you aware that a number of women and children were killed in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Whenever I visited the doctor at Stari Vitez, she would always tell me what had happened since the last visit. This was when they would always want to show me the dead bodies, to prove to me that this had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see dead bodies in there?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of women?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Of men and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what was your conclusion at the time of the nature of the military campaign being waged against Stari Vitez by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It appeared to be more of a containment campaign, not to try and seize and hold the ground of Stari Vitez, but more to ensure that the occupants of Stari Vitez didn't expand their enclave or attempt to break out of their enclave. It was more static, more containment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What about in respect of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: We were allowed under control to take aid in and to evacuate people out, but with some of the weapons that were used, the mortars and the blast bombs, it appeared to be indiscriminate, rather than aimed at the actual front-lines where the majority of the Bosnian army soldiers would be in Stari Vitez. These blast weapons actually were landing in more the centre of Stari Vitez, and because of their nature, caused civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was a process of attrition of the population in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It psychologically and physically wore down the will of the population of Stari Vitez because they relied totally on aid agencies and myself to evacuate wounded people and to take aid in. They had no method at all of getting assistance in any vehicle whatsoever. It had to be brought in by an aid agency. So the military campaign combined with the control of access to Stari Vitez by agencies, such as myself and the Red Cross and the UNHCR, seemed to be this containment and gradual wearing down, keeping the enclave at a low ebb, a low level of ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why do you think the HVO, as it were, had this policy of containment of this pocket within the Vitez town?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I believed that it was an implied threat to the Bosnian Army 3 Corps, in Zenica and also to the Bosnian Army 325 Brigade which was based around the Chadras Poculica area just north of the Vitez area, that if any attempt was made to attack the Vitez area and relieve Stari Vitez, that Stari Vitez would suffer considerable damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did the people not just leave? Why did the Muslims not just leave Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: A number of reasons. I think a lot of them didn't want to leave, despite the conditions they were forced to live in, because they knew that if they voluntarily left their homes, the UNHCR would describe them as displaced people and not refugees so, therefore, would not be accorded the same level of aid as a refugee, because they had left voluntarily their homes where they had shelter. It was also where their families were and there were young and old. It was a question of where could they go? I visited the refugees from Ahmici in Zenica which they were housed in the old bunkers, the air raid bunkers in Zenica, and they were in appalling conditions, living in the bunkers with no windows, in large rooms sleeping on the floor. And I don't think the people of Stari Vitez wanted to be treated like that. They also, I feel, felt that they would be in risk or danger if they did try to leave. They could be either shot at or beaten when they attempted to leave and that they wouldn't be able to take a great deal of personal belongings with them. So there was a split of opinion as to why they wouldn't want to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far was the Hotel Vitez from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I would say no more than 500, 600 metres from the front-line of Stari Vitez. It was, in my vehicle, 30 seconds to a minute to get from Hotel Vitez into the Bosnian army controlled area of Stari Vitez. It was very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This campaign that fluctuated, as you said, but went on for a six-month period, would it be possible for those in Hotel Vitez not to be aware of what was going on around Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I would find it difficult to believe that people physically in Hotel Vitez would not hear the mortars or the fire extinguisher bombs or the rifle fire when it occurred, and from my own personal experience, if you hear a mortar or artillery round or small arms fire near you, your natural question is: Which way is it travelling? Is it travelling away from me or towards me? As a military commander, I would expect the people in Hotel Vitez to want to know if it was the Bosnian army firing their weapons at the Croat population of Vitez or the other way around because Croatian casualties, HVO casualties, were caused by the Bosnian army faction in Stari Vitez because I evacuated some of them from the Vitez hospital as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the degree of coordination, in your opinion, of this campaign of sniping and firing of these indiscriminate weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: There seemed to be a progression of this campaign. Initially, in May, it was infrequent, and it seemed to follow the level of fighting elsewhere in the Lasva Valley, and it fluctuated. But there appeared to be, in July and August, a concerted increase in the number of incidents and casualties caused. To some degree, on the 18th, 19th of July, I was unable to evacuate casualties for a period of maybe 30 hours because the fighting was too intense for me to get into Stari Vitez, but we had been told that there were as many as 16 casualties in Stari Vitez that required assistance. So it fluctuated from sporadic to intense, and then it would ease off, and then it would increase again over the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the Bosnian forces that were located in Stari Vitez. What was the degree of their ability to actually fight out of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I didn't personally deal with the Bosnian army in Stari Vitez. It was not my role. But in my opinion, they could contain their pocket, but I don't think they had the ability to sustain a long assault out of Stari Vitez, and I think that the will to do so was minimal because of the number of civilians that were inside Stari Vitez, that they ultimately would have to leave if they tried to break out, and they obviously would or could suffer as casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, one last question in this area. Did you ever supply ammunition or weapons to the Bosnian forces in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move ahead with your testimony, and if the map that was in front of the witness could be placed back in front of him? Now, very briefly, can you explain to the Judges, and you've touched upon it already, your visit to Kruscica I think throughout May of 1993. No, the map, this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I was attempting to get an aid convoy to Kruscica here in May (indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're indicating the circle marked 4.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: And it was the normal practice for the women and children of that area to stand and block the road. These were still in the HVO part of the Lasva Valley, close to the front-line with the Bosnian army at Kruscica, and they would engage me in a series of demands as to why I couldn't take the convoys through, and these ranged from no aid being given to the HVO in Vitez, that I was taking weapons through and ammunition to the Bosnian part of Kruscica, and it was always the women and children that would block the road with a number of HVO soldiers to the side of the road, one of them who I ended up speaking to regularly was called Captain Nikola, and it appeared to me that they were directing what the women and children were doing. It got to the degree of "The weapons are in your vehicles," so after an hour or so, we would let them look in the back of the UNHCR vehicle. They would say, "The ammunition is in the boxes, in the food parcels." So we would say, "Pick a box. Open it." And then it would be, "The ammunition is in the tins of food or in the parcels of food." So every time we tried to accommodate their demands, the demand would move. The final argument as to why we couldn't go through was because they had been shown a video of UNPROFOR troops distributing weapons and ammunition to the Bosnian army. I specifically asked Captain Nikola to show me this video or to tell me where this video had come from or who it involved, because it appeared to be a very serious stumbling block with a lot of the local people around Vitez. But over a period of ten days, he was unable to show me this video. And, again, while I was discussing the events with him, conversations would be going on around me, and again my interpreter, Dobrilla Kolaba, told me that she had heard that this video didn't actually exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this place that you were trying to get to was a partial Muslim enclave?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could it gain supplies from any other source apart from international aid agencies?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I believe there was limited access from the south into Kruscica, but the aid agencies didn't use this route, so there was limited access for re-supply but not for large quantities of aid, in the region of 25 tonnes, which was required on a regular basis, or for the evacuation of casualties because they needed to go to Zenica which was to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you believe that the HVO were manipulating the civilian population to prevent your access to the area of the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, and it was very, very effective. It would make the U.N. and other aid agencies and UNPROFOR look very bad if we tried to force our way through a human blockade of women and children, and on a number of occasions, the international media were there when we were attempting to negotiate aid through these checkpoints. On one occasion very early on, I did try to walk in front of my vehicle, my Land Rover, to see if we could just go through and they would move away from the road, but as soon as we started the engine and started to drive forward, the HVO soldiers to the side shot over our heads which, to me, was a clear indication that I should stop what I was doing and go back to negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move ahead, and this is the part of your testimony where I think you say a number of things in your statement about what you were aware of were known as HOS units in the Lasva Valley. I wonder if you can tell the Judges what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The initial briefs which were given to us on arrival in Bosnia informed us of various units and sub-units within the area, both Bosnian army and HVO. One of the units mentioned was called HOS. A general description was given of what they looked like so we could identify them if we saw them. I tended to see these units in very small groups but only in passing. I had no direct requirement to speak to them. I generally saw them and recognised them because of their dress. They wore very dark blue or black clothing, some had white belts with a cross-belt over their chest, some would have badges with the letters spelling "HOS" on them. They had pistols rather than long-barrelled rifles, and they tended to drive Western European cars, one that I particularly remember was a dark blue Volkswagen Golf where I remember seeing frequently around the roads between the Novi Travnik T-junction, which is up here (indicated), to the Busovaca T-junction and the road towards Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How well-supplied did these individuals appear to you?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: The fact that they had fuel for the cars which we saw them in indicated to me that they had access to the more sought-after logistics. We were constantly being asked to provide fuel for the generators at the Novi Bila hospital, which we did, but if fuel was in such short supply for something as important as a hospital, there were -- the majority of the cars which we saw driving about were not by the -- I would call it the everyday population. They tended to be the important people, the civilian politicians, the military commanders, or the more favoured military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it the battalion's view that these HOS units were commanded by the HVO at the time that you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was the general impression that we had, that they weren't restricted by a geographical area but, ultimately, the chain of command would lead to Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see HOS and HVO soldiers together at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. There appeared to be just general talking, as if they were talking to people that they knew. They never tried to take over the checkpoint commander's duties. They just appeared to be talking, smoking, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they allowed to freely pass through HVO checkpoints, HOS, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: They didn't seem to be restricted in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And many other people were restricted in their movements in that area by HVO checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I don't know if I would say "restricted." I think there was a necessity, a military necessity, to keep an idea of who was moving around the main roads. In any war, you're going to want to know who is transiting your routes, so I think it was more that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever see HOS units setting up snap checkpoints themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I saw them stopping and talking to people on the roads. Obviously, I don't know what they were talking about, but it just appeared to be just general talking to them, I mean, inquiring as to where they were going. Invariably they were -- the HOS had a car, and the people were either walking or they had carts or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of these HOS individuals or units in and around Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I think I can recollect maybe one or two in the car park, but I never saw any inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move on now very briefly to Dobrilla Kolaba, who was your interpreter and who was shot. I'm sure you can recall the date that she was shot.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: She was shot on Monday, the 5th of July, at about half past eight in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By whom was she shot? What was the group consensus about that?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: She was shot by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that she was actually standing underneath a huge U.N. blue flag at the time that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The house where she lived was a house rented from a family for the U.N., it was known as the captains' house, and all the BRITBAT captains, liaison officers, lived in that house, and also Dobrilla Kolaba had a room in that house as well. Early on, it was apparent that if we didn't identify that house and other houses habitated by U.N. personnel, that there was a danger of receiving gunfire or blast injuries or whatever, so we got hold of large U.N. flags, I would say slightly bigger than the flags which are in this court now, and it was hung on the veranda, the balcony, which was above where she was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can move on now to your observation of individuals digging trenches, and if you can point on the map to the area with which we're concerned for this part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It's here, Area 5, which was north of Novi Travnik (indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is again, I think, on Exhibit 394. Could you recollect that event to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: At the time the main transit route from Busovaca to Travnik, up here, was very close to an offensive by the Bosnian army and was deemed unsafe. The Red Cross had negotiated passage through the HVO front-lines north of Travnik and the Bosnian army front-lines south of Travnik to take an aid convoy into Travnik. Because the road was mountainous and it caused a strain on the vehicles and there may be a danger from the fighting, we accompanied the convoy, at the rear of it, so that we had communications with our own base that if there was a problem, we could get assistance for the Red Cross. At the time, their radio communications were not as reliable as ours. We were approaching the front-line of the HVO because I could see the mortar weapon -- pits where they dug their mortars into and some trenches and what looked like command bunkers, and I saw a number, 15, I don't think any more than 15, men in civilian clothes. They looked fairly dirty and dishevelled, untidy, and they were digging what looks like large trench systems. There were a number of HVO soldiers with weapons who were sat down, stood around, and watching the people dig. All the people were digging at one time as opposed to what I would normally expect: Some would dig, some would stand around, and whatever. They were all digging. And the soldiers were looking at -- they were facing south, so they were looking at the diggers, they weren't facing towards the front-line. I slowed down in the vehicle to get a better look, and hand gestures were given by the soldiers that I should carry on. I didn't want to restrict the ICRC's passage using that route, so I didn't want to make an issue out of it. I just informed the Red Cross, had they seen it, and I let them deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did these people look like volunteers to you?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: They weren't enthusiastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now moving to the final part of your examination-in-chief and the attack that you witnessed on the village of Grbavica. First of all, can you explain to the Judges where Grbavica is located, particularly in relation to your camp, the BRITBAT camp? I think it's marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It's here as Area 6. The small circle at the top is the high ground. It was a high feature which rose from the road, which was almost in a valley, and the hill rose up towards the circle (indicated). The majority of the houses were in this shape here (indicated) and the majority of the Bosnian army trench systems were around this circle on the high ground. The BRITBAT base was here; it was overlooked by the high ground. We were about here (indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, as I said, in September of 1993, you witnessed an attack by the HVO on Grbavica, and I wonder, can you describe that to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: I only witnessed the beginnings of the attack. It appeared to be a professional, well-coordinated military offensive to seize and hold an area of ground. The troops, the HVO forces, used recoilless rifles -- they're a bigger calibre, have an explosive impact when they reach their target -- and they started at one end and cleared, systematically, house by house. There were some Croat families living in the village and their houses remained untouched, but the Muslim population were cleared out of their houses by the progression of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, were any houses set on fire during this attack, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: There were a number which tended to be near the top of the hill feature, and one or two in this area here, just by the road (indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have a couple of photographs that I will place on the ELMO when you have finished this part of your testimony. Now, once the Muslim forces and the Muslim civilians had been cleared out, what happened to these civilians, these Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: They congregated around the entrance to the British Battalion camp in two houses and they pleaded to be let into the camp, but we had a policy of not letting anyone into the camp for fear that once they were in, they would not leave, and I believe this had happened in Kakanj to another UNPROFOR unit, and it created a problem. So anyone that turned up that had any weapons or military equipment, the liaison officers that were there disarmed them and separated them from their weapons and told them, if they had any other clothes, to change out of their military equipment and all stay in the two houses next to the British camp and we would try and protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it the view that the civilians amongst these people were in grave risk of being killed?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: They were caught up in a battle, and therefore were at risk. One man was shot dead in front of two liaison officers as they were discussing evacuating the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, immediately after the attack had been completed, the people cleared out, did looting commence?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Initially, it was by HVO soldiers. They were taking electrical items, furniture. And shortly afterwards, Croat families moved into the houses that were now unoccupied, and there seemed to be a redistribution of the property of those houses, and that was being done by non-combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that some HVO soldiers actually entered the BRITBAT captains' house and got rather a shock, I think, when they attempted to start looting?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: We had been working for maybe 36 hours, so when the fighting finished, we all went back to our house; and while we were there, two soldiers, HVO soldiers, came into the house, one was drunk, and they claimed they were having a look around, but they were asked to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, indeed, I think they left?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the last two photographs, that's 396 and 397, if the map could be left there because there's one place that I failed to identify, which I will. What does this first photograph show?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: This is a photograph I took of the southern edge of Grbavica looking directly north towards the high ground which you can see up here. The BRITBAT camp was over the hill in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what stage is this photograph, at what time; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: This photograph, I think, I took in late September/October time. I couldn't say the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could place Exhibit 397? If you could indicate to the Judges the location of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: This is the high ground here to the left and it's looking down the feature. This is now looking -- the pointer is moving south, and the main road which would go from Travnik to Busovaca is in this direction here. This is the entranceway to the BRITBAT camp and this is Grbavica around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there's a couple of houses on the top of the feature with roofs that are missing which, perhaps, are the houses that you referred to that had been burned?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just point those out?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: There at the top here, and there were a number down here on the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That had been burned?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: That had been burned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the map could be placed back on the ELMO now, please, finally? Could you just move it so the number "2" is there? Sorry, my mistake, Major Bower, I failed to mention this. Can you identify the area marked "2"?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: This area here is right on the edge of the Busovaca to Travnik road on a bend. It's maybe 500, 600 metres from the cemetery which is down here, and it was a chalet/lodge type accommodation, building. When we first arrived in Bosnia, it was used, we believe, by the group known as the Jokeri.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That was the group that was described earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was the group which I encountered down here which was to the west of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, finally, I think in October of 1993, just before the end of your tour, you were ordered to go to the village of Stupni Do in the municipality of Vares?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe very briefly to the court what you found in that village when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It was total destruction of the village. There were very few houses that had not been set on fire and totally destroyed. There were a number of bodies in the area, and the ones which stick in my mind are the two women which had been shot as they hid in the vegetable pit in one of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was your access to the village of Stupni Do controlled?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: We didn't have too much difficulty entering the village. We were there fairly quickly after the attack had taken place. We were there for some 18 hours, but when I tried to leave before the remainder of the UNPROFOR troops, there was a checkpoint at the bottom of the mountain road south of Stupni Do where I had an anti-armour rocket launcher pointed at my vehicle. The soldiers had made their weapons ready to fire and they were very agitated, appeared very nervous, and they didn't want me to leave at all. They wanted to know what we had been doing up there, what we had seen and where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these were HVO soldiers at this checkpoint with the anti-armour rocket?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The village of Stupni Do was a Bosnian Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly returning to sniping, and this is really an opinion of what you observed in Stari Vitez, what is the psychological effect of a sniping campaign on civilians, women and children?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER
utterances.text: It will be psychologically damaging to any group of people. Even military formations can be demoralises by the effective use of a sniping campaign. It was effective to the degree that many in Stari Vitez would not travel outside their houses during the heat of the fighting during daylight hours. They would remain in cover. They were extremely frightened of becoming casualties themselves. So a lot of their home-grown foods, their root vegetables, couldn't be gathered during daylight hours; water couldn't be collected. They were restricted to the very centre of Stari Vitez where they knew they were not in line of sight of any HVO positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. If I could apply for admission into evidence of 394, 395, 396 and 397?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. At this point and further to what we said yesterday, I think I'd like to have a pause first, but ask the Defence before we do take our break about how much time they plan to take. I'm not going to try to limit them in any way. Mr. Hayman or Mr. Nobilo, can you give us an idea of how long you need and, if necessary, we will have the Major come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. President, this witness has touched on a lot of different topics and it's a new time period in the case. This is not the tour of the Cheshire Regiment. This is the tour of the Prince of Wales own. So I would expect my cross-examination to be less than the direct but still perhaps go for two hours or even a little more. I also have some documents to show the witness, so if we're going to conclude by 1.30, I don't think that will be possible. And I would like to raise the question with the court if it wants me to start and then interrupt the cross and continue it in three weeks or if the court would rather have the examination all at once. I leave it entirely to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. Perhaps you would like to work without stopping, though. I suppose you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if Judge Shahabuddeen will be back. That may be hard for him if he has not heard the direct. I think it's generally preferable that direct and cross all be together but it all be concluded at once. I don't know if this witness can be back when we start in three weeks. Particularly, if he can't be back in three weeks but he may be coming back at some other time and not be the first witness, then it might be best to have the cross-examination all at once, whenever it's convenient to the witness but I leave it to the court. We also want to use the available time, so we have mixed feelings about the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we have to put the question of Judge Shahabuddeen aside. We have a presiding officer here. Judge Shahabuddeen will know everything that has been said through the transcripts and the exhibits. I have to isolate that. That's a separate issue. When he comes back from Tanzania, he will be operational once again and can be here for the cross-examination. What I find particularly problematic, but I wanted to have your opinion, the Defence, I would like to ask the Prosecution as well, I suppose there's no problem in having the Major come back; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, the witness is available to the court. Obviously I would have to speak to him about dates and times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We said it yesterday, and when I thanked the interpreters, they shown that they've been willing to work very hard. We are going to take a twenty-minute break. The question is to know whether we are going to stop now or whether we should begin with the cross-examination and continue to 1.30, but we won't go beyond 1.30. I said it yesterday, even though perhaps the witness wouldn't even be here in September, our schedule will be more set. Each party wants to exercise its rights as completely as possible. The witness was supposed to talk an hour. He spoke an hour and 45 minutes. I didn't interrupt him. I don't want to interrupt the witnesses. I'm simply noting that that's how things are. But it is out of the question as well to prevent the Defence exercising its right to cross-examination. I will consult with my colleague and then we will rediscuss the issue. We have looked at all possibilities, Judge Riad and myself. I think we have to be logical. That's the procedural way of working. There is the Defence logic, the Prosecution logic, the interpreter's logic, the Judges' logic, all kinds of logic. We could have gone on until 2.00 if necessary, but it seems to me that the Defence really cannot commit itself to say that it is going to be finished by 2.00. We do agree with that, Mr. Hayman; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I cannot render a scientific precision. I will certainly do my best but it is not a scientific matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Also, I have some scruples to ask more from the interpreters than I've already committed myself to. I've entered into a contract with them and I don't want to not respect it. That's how things are. Very well. I think that we have to be realistic, and what I suggest is that we have two solutions. The Defence is the one who will choose, and I think the Defence will choose. As we take a 20-minute break until twenty after, that is the contract that I entered into with the interpreters for Fridays and Mondays. Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo, General Blaskic, you have a choice.
